sub: Named after masad, “palm fibre”, in ayah 5; also known as Al-Lahab
theme: The only place the Quran condemns an enemy of the Prophet ﷺ by name: his own uncle, Abū Lahab. His wealth and children cannot save him, and he and his wife will burn in the Fire.
story: Revealed in Makkah. Abū Lahab, real name ʿAbd al-ʿUzzā, was the Prophet’s ﷺ uncle and next-door neighbour, yet his bitterest opponent. He followed him through the markets, telling people: “He is a liar, don’t listen to him.”

When told to warn his nearest relatives, the Prophet ﷺ climbed Ṣafā and called the clans of Quraysh: “If I told you an enemy was about to attack, would you believe me?” They said yes. “Then I warn you of a severe punishment.”

Abū Lahab snapped: “May you perish! Is this why you gathered us?” The surah came in reply. Both he and his wife, who also harmed the Prophet ﷺ, were alive when it came, and neither ever accepted Islam.

sections.title: Abū Lahab’s wealth won’t save him; he and his wife will burn
sections.meaning: Abū Lahab’s hands are ruined, and he is ruined. His wealth and what he earned, including his children, will not help him. He will burn in a flaming Fire, and so will his wife, the carrier of firewood, with a rope of twisted fibre on her neck.
points: May Abū Lahab’s hands perish, and he has perished
His wealth and earnings won’t help him
He will burn in a Fire of flame
His wife too, carrying firewood, a fibre rope on her neck
sections.matters: Family ties do not replace faith: the Prophet’s ﷺ own uncle is condemned by name. It also showed people that Abū Lahab’s attacks came from hatred, and that no relative gets special treatment in this religion.
sections.story: At Ṣafā, the Prophet ﷺ warned Quraysh of a severe punishment. Abū Lahab replied, “May you perish! Is this why you gathered us?”, and reportedly picked up a stone to throw at him. Other reports give different occasions.
explained: Tabbat yadā: may his hands be ruined. The hands stand for the whole person, since they do most deeds. Wa-tabb: and he is ruined, first a prayer against him, then news that it came true. Mā kasab, “what he earned”, includes his children. He had boasted they would ransom him.

He will burn in a Fire dhāt lahab, full of flame, echoing his nickname, Abū Lahab. His wife Umm Jamīl joins him. Ḥammālat al-ḥaṭab: she scattered thorny branches in the Prophet’s ﷺ path, or carried gossip to kindle hatred. On her neck is a rope of masad: palm fibre, or twisted iron.
teaches: Being related to a righteous person saves no one; faith and deeds do.
Wealth and children cannot protect anyone from Allah’s punishment.
Carrying gossip to stir up hatred is a grave sin.
Opposing the truth ends in loss, however powerful the opponent.
sections.hook: Lahab, “flame”, appears twice: in his name, Abū Lahab (1), and in the Fire, dhāt lahab (3). Tabb comes twice in ayah 1. The last word, masad, names the surah.

groups.text: Abū Lahab is ruined, and his wealth and children will not help him.
He will burn in a Fire full of flames.
So will his wife, the carrier of firewood, with a rope of palm fibre around her neck.

1.explain: Tabbat yadā Abī Lahab: may his hands be ruined, meaning the whole man. Wa-tabb: and ruined he is. The first is a prayer against him, the second states it came true. He died about a week after Badr.
1.why: At Ṣafā the Prophet ﷺ warned Quraysh of a coming punishment, and Abū Lahab said: “May you perish! Is this why you gathered us?” Other reports: he asked what extra he would get for believing, or told visitors the Prophet ﷺ was a liar.

2.explain: Mā aghnā: of no use to him. Neither his wealth nor mā kasab, what he earned, will shield him. Mā kasab is said to mean his children, since children are part of a man’s earnings.
2.why: When the Prophet ﷺ warned his relatives, Abū Lahab reportedly said: “If what my nephew says is true, I will ransom myself with my wealth and my children.”

3.explain: Sa-yaṣlā: he will burn in a Fire dhāt lahab, full of flames surrounding him on every side. It echoes his nickname, Abū Lahab, “father of flame”, given for his glowing, reddish face.

4.explain: His wife, Umm Jamīl, sister of Abū Sufyān, helped him harm the Prophet ﷺ. Ḥammālat al-ḥaṭab: she scattered thorns in his path, or spread gossip to kindle hatred, or will carry fuel to her husband’s Fire.

5.explain: Fī jīdihā: on her neck. Ḥablun min masad: a rope of twisted palm fibre, or, in the Fire, a chain of twisted iron.
